column4: ch-001.txt title page and preface
column5: Course (Module 3 worked example, C4 answer key, real-evidence line) cites the 1845 tract Religious Instruction of Negroes. Title page reads 'Savannah: Published by Thomas Purse. 1842' and copyright entry is 1842; the preface is dated July 1842. Trust the source: 1842.

column4: ch-001.txt Contents, Part III II.3
column5: Jones (a Presbyterian minister in Georgia, writing for slaveholders) lists the objections his readers raised, including that religious instruction would produce insubordination and that 'Negroes will embrace seasons of religious worship for originating and executing plans of insubordination'. Those are the fears that the Willie Lynch letter dramatises. Use as a primary example of slaveholder anxieties, paraphrased, with the author's pro-slavery aims stated.

column4: ch-001.txt preface
column5: Author's own description of the book's aim: 'to speak the truth plainly and in love', written for the 'Christian Public'. Cite it as a pro-slavery apologia, the way Garvey or Moyo are cited, not as neutral history.

column4: ch-002.txt Part I ch.1, 1712 New York conspiracy
column5: Jones records that in 1712 Negroes in New York conspired against the English, and that the catechising school of Elias Neau was blamed. He says the guilty men were 'such as never came to Mr. Neau's school', and that anti-instruction masters were the ones whose slaves were most guilty. This is a planters' argument against instruction, recorded from a church history. Use only as a documented instance of the blame argument.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.1 para 1
column5: Jones dates the first arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia to August 1620, from a Dutch man-of-war. Most modern sources date it to 1619 (White Lion). Check any date the course gives for the first arrival against the 1619 record before using Jones's date.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.1, Bishop of London letter 1727
column5: The 1727 Bishop of London letter to masters (quoted by Jones) argues that baptism does not change a person's civil status and that Christian instruction makes slaves more dutiful. It also urges masters to teach the 'Negroes' and says severity is needed only where 'the want of religion' leaves people ungoverned. A useful primary voice for how church and master argued over conversion. Paraphrase only.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.1 Georgia 1747 resolutions
column5: Jones quotes the 1747 Georgia assembly resolutions that owners 'should educate the young' and that acts of inhumanity 'should be punished by the civil authority'. A primary-source example of the legal recognition of slavery in Georgia alongside a claim of duties to the enslaved. Note the claim of duty is recorded as a resolution, not evidence of practice.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.1 Samuel Davies 1755 and 1757 letters
column5: Presbyterian Samuel Davies in Hanover, Virginia, reported to London in 1755 about 100 baptised enslaved adults and about 300 attending regularly, and in 1757 about 150 baptised. Jones cites these as evidence that enslaved people sought instruction. Each figure is the minister's own report, not a count by an independent body.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 Andrew Bryan, Savannah, 1788-1793
column5: Jones records that Andrew Bryan, an enslaved preacher in Savannah, was punished with stripes and imprisoned for holding meetings. He was later allowed to preach under civil regulations, and in 1788 Abraham Marshall ordained him and constituted the first colored Baptist church in Savannah with 69 members. Jones cites a later 1812 letter by Holcombe. Use as a documented example of religious leadership by enslaved people under legal repression. Paraphrase; the punishment account is from Jones and Holcombe, not court records.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 Methodist returns
column5: Jones gives Methodist returns of 'colored members' (1786: 1,890; 1787: 3,893; 1790: 11,682; 1796: 11,220). These are the only denominational counts he has, and he says the other churches kept none. Use the figures only with that caveat.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 1816 AME secession
column5: Jones, quoting Bangs, records the 1816 secession of Philadelphia's Black Methodists under Richard Allen, who was elected bishop of the new African Methodist Episcopal Church, and says the Southern slave membership stayed with white ministers because they were 'pledged' to good behaviour. A primary-source reference for the AME founding; prefer a dedicated history for the date and details.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 1820 census figures and 1822-23 North Carolina school ban
column5: Jones gives census totals (1800: 893,041 slaves and 110,555 free; 1810: 1,191,364 and 195,643; 1820: 1,538,064 and 244,020) and reports a North Carolina law forbidding school instruction for Black people, which he places in the Moravian account of 1822-23. Check the year of the NC law in a legal history before quoting it as 1823.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 1833 synod resolutions
column5: The 1833 synod of South Carolina and Georgia resolved to 'separate entirely the civil and religious condition' of enslaved people, to improve the religious condition while disclaiming 'all interference with the former', and to instruct only 'as permitted by the laws of the States'. A primary-source statement of the 'religion without freedom' position, quotable in short form (under 15 words) with attribution.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.2 1835 synod report
column5: A 1835 synod report blames 'the lamentable interference of abolition fanatics' for suspending instruction in some parts of the country. Use as an example of how slaveholders framed abolitionists, paraphrased, with the author's view noted.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.3 1840-41 Methodist and Sunbury Baptist counts
column5: Jones gives Methodist colored communicants as 94,532 (1840) and 102,158 (1841), and says Methodist missions reported about 6,145 members in South Carolina in 1841. Figures are from the church minutes he quotes and are church returns, not census counts.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.3 Jones's own northern observations, 1827-1839
column5: Jones, who wrote as a Georgia pastor, reports his own visits to Providence, Boston, New York and Philadelphia (1827, 1829, 1839) and describes Black quarters there as crowded and poor. He uses the picture to argue for instruction and against the free states; the observation is his own and unverified. Use only with that caveat.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.3 concluding general observations
column5: Jones concludes that the 1830s northern anti-slavery petitions and publications turned the South 'from the salvation of the soul' to the defence of political rights, and that this halted instruction. He also writes that 'the people have consequently been left ... in moral darkness'. A primary statement of how slaveholding churches explained the decline. Quotable as a short phrase only.

column4: ch-002.txt ch.3 census totals
column5: Arithmetic checked: 1830 colored population 2,009,043 slave + 319,599 free = 2,328,642 (matches Jones). 1840: 2,487,113 + 386,235 = 2,873,348 (matches). Use these totals if a course figure needs a US Black population for 1830 or 1840.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.1 'hardening effect' of management
column5: Jones, a slaveholder, admits that managing enslaved people 'hardening' the manager's heart and that masters 'cherish ... a disrespect, if not a contempt' for those they manage. A rare first-hand admission, from inside slaveholding, of how the system shaped the owner. Use paraphrased, as evidence of the system's effect on owners.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.1 race taxonomy
column5: Jones uses a racial hierarchy ('Caucasian' at the head, 'Ethiopian' at the foot) and calls the difference 'the fact'. Good example of 1840s racial science used to justify slavery. Cite as period language, not as a reading of the Africans' own history.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.2 literacy bans
column5: Jones, writing as a slaveholder in 1842, states that the statutes of the slave states 'forbid all knowledge of letters to the Negroes', and that custom did the rest. A primary attestation of the literacy bans, from the defenders of slavery themselves. Use this with the state statutes, not alone.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.2 claims of superstition and 'easy dupes'
column5: Jones writes that enslaved people, 'ignorance and superstition render them easy dupes' to conjurers, and that they believed in charms making them invulnerable. This is the planter's view of the people he owned, used as evidence about them. It supports the hoax's logic ('keep them ignorant and superstitious') and should be cited only as the planter's claim, never as a reliable account of enslaved belief. Use with that caveat if at all.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.3 'vices' list and Jones's own causes
column5: Chapter III lists 'prevailing vices' (theft, falsehood, drunkenness, marriage breakdown) as the planter's view. Jones himself names the causes: no legal protection for marriage, no literacy, no family government, sales and division of families. Use his causal statements (paraphrased) as evidence that slavery shaped these conditions. Do not cite the vice claims as facts about the people.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.3 pro-slavery quotations, Dalcho 1823 and Pinckney 1829
column5: Jones quotes pro-slavery writers: Dalcho (1823) says 'ages and generations must pass away' before enslaved people could be made virtuous; Pinckney (1829) calls plantation morals a 'doctrine of human depravity'. Use only as examples of slavery's defenders, in paraphrase, with the date and author.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.3 prison-statistics extracts
column5: Jones's extracts include Ohio, Connecticut and Massachusetts prison statistics from the 1830s used to argue that free Black people were more criminal. Those are the ratios of convicts to the population in each state, as quoted, and the figures show the proportions of Black people in prison without context. Do not use them as evidence of character.

column4: ch-003.txt ch.3 general conclusions 1842
column5: Jones's final conclusions: Black Americans are 'intellectually and morally a degraded people', 'may with propriety be termed the heathen of our land', and are 'left in next to absolute dependence upon ... the whites'. A clear statement of the slaveholding church's view in 1842; quotable only in short paraphrase with the author named.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.1 control of access to the Gospel
column5: Jones admits that slaveholders could 'forbid religious meetings', decide which churches enslaved people attend, and that 'all approaches to them from abroad are rigidly guarded against', with Black preachers 'discouraged, if not suppressed'. A first-hand statement that the church's access to the enslaved was controlled by owners. Strong evidence for the lesson on control.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.1 use of scripture
column5: Jones argues from Genesis 17, Deuteronomy and Ephesians 6 and Colossians 4 that masters are commanded to instruct enslaved people, and uses Abraham and Job as models. This is the scriptural justification for religious instruction as a master's duty. Cite as an example of how Christian slaveholders used scripture, not as a reading of the texts.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.2 excuses and the 'incapable' argument
column5: Jones lists slaveholders' excuses for not instructing enslaved people, including that they are 'incapable' of instruction, and answers that the Gospel is intelligible to all people. He then concedes that inequality may exist 'between the races' and calls it no impeachment of God. The chapter shows that the 'incapacity' claim was common in the 1840s and was disputed inside the slaveholding church too. Quote as a documented contemporary argument.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.2 Jones on the free states and emancipation
column5: Jones says that in parts of Rhode Island, New Jersey, New York and Delaware, formerly Black communities had 'melted away' after emancipation. He offers this as an argument against emancipation. The statement is his claim with no numbers. Treat as a documented claim, not a finding.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.3 separation principle, Romans 13 and 1 Corinthians 7
column5: Jones restates the 'separation' principle: the church handles 'their religious condition' while disclaiming any interference in 'their civil condition', citing 'render unto Caesar'. He also reads 1 Corinthians 7:21 as Paul advising slaves to take freedom if they can. The verse is disputed; cite Jones's reading as his reading only.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.3 'get all, give back as little' principle
column5: Jones reports the master-servant relation as the principle 'get all, and give back as little as you can' on the master's side and the reverse on the servant's side, and calls it 'pure selfishness'. A candid slaveholder description of the bargain of the system. Paraphrase only.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.3 self-reported plantation work
column5: Jones says that over about eight years he led 'five or six hundred meetings upon plantations', with crowds of 20 to 500, and was disturbed only three times. This is his own self-report, uncorroborated. Use only as his claim.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.4 list of revolts 1712 to 1832
column5: Jones lists revolts and plots (New York 1712; South Carolina 1730 and 1739; New York 1741; Camden 1816; Charleston 1822; Southampton 'in 1832'). He attributes several to religion or to Spanish agents, and says the 1822 Charleston plot used the Bible. A slaveholder's account of rebellion, with his attributions. Cite as his claim; the revolts themselves are attested separately.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.4 date of Southampton revolt
column5: Jones dates the Southampton rising (Nat Turner's revolt) to 1832. The revolt took place in August 1831. Check any date before quoting Jones on it.

column4: ch-004.txt ch.4 1712 New York plot as cited in Jones
column5: Jones gives the 1712 New York plot twice (ch-002 and ch-004), with the same quotation from Neau's school. Coincidentally the Willie Lynch letter is dated 1712. Do not treat the shared year as evidence for the letter. Jones's 1712 account is a real event with a documented school dispute.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.1-2 the plan: church-based instruction
column5: Part IV sets out a plan for church-run instruction: presbytery reports, Sabbath schools, catechising children, and church-recorded marriages. It is the policy the synods had adopted. Jones's plan keeps the civil condition untouched, as in Part III. Cite as the official 1840s church policy, not as a record of what happened.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.2 owner's plan: paternalism and punishment
column5: Jones's plan for owners includes gardens and poultry for enslaved families, 'as little resort to corporal chastisement as possible', and sending children to Sabbath school 'in charge of ... the driver'. It is a written paternalist programme for plantations, showing the owner's authority over how families lived. Use as a primary source for the paternalist ideology of the 1840s, paraphrased.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.2 missionary costs
column5: Jones gives the costs of supporting a plantation missionary (about $100 a year, shared by ten planters at $50 each) and says some plantations with net incomes of $10,000 to $30,000 gave $25 to $100 for religious instruction. These are his figures, unsourced. Use only with that caveat.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.3 minister's rule: no talk of owners' civil condition
column5: Jones tells ministers to 'hear no tales at all respecting owners and matters which belong to their civil condition', citing Luke 12:13-14. This is the separation principle put as a rule for preachers: the church may discuss souls but not the system. Good primary evidence of how instruction was bounded by owners' interests, paraphrased.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.3 controls on plantation meetings
column5: Jones sets rules for plantation meetings: the owner must consent, the owner decides who may attend, and 'a collection of Negroes from several plantations ... at night ... ought not to be allowed'. A written control rule from the period, showing how instruction was made dependent on owners. Paraphrase only.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.3 Jones as author of a catechism
column5: Jones names as his own a 'Catechism of Scripture Doctrine and Practice, designed for the oral instruction of colored persons'. He is the author of one of the manuals he recommends, so his evidence on instruction is partly his own work. Note this when citing him on what worked.

column4: ch-005.txt ch.3 mixed churches and subordination
column5: Jones argues that white and Black members should worship in the same church under the same pastor in the slave states, because mixing 'tends to increase subordination'. A primary statement of why the church preferred integrated congregations there. Paraphrase only.
